prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical discovery of the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize on B006 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The scientific case is that time-reversal symmetry together with spin-orbit coupling gives a Z2 classification of band insulators, and that this classification predicts protected edge and surface states that were then observed. That is a new organising principle for electronic matter, not a technique. The first experimental test, Molenkamp's HgTe quantum wells, was unambiguous, and about two decades of transport, photoemission and tunnelling work by independent groups have left the interpretation stable. In answer to the chair's question, my one-sentence distinction from 2016 is this: the 2016 prize recognised topological invariants in one-dimensional chains and in the quantum Hall effect, where time-reversal symmetry is broken by a magnetic field, while the Z2 insulator is a zero-field, time-reversal-invariant state whose protection comes from spin-orbit coupling in ordinary band structure. That difference is what turned topology into something that first-principles materials calculations could search for and classify. On attribution, all six supporters now name the same trio, and I think Kane and Mele are inseparable because the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall prediction are a joint result. For the citation, I would write it around the 2D quantum spin Hall state and its HgTe observation, so that it does not imply that the 3D materials discovery is being recognised.
statement.case_against: The cost of this configuration is real and I do not want to hide it behind the count of supporters. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested, and Zhang's death means he cannot be recognised in any case. Hasan's photoemission work established the 3D strand, alongside Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy, and a three-name limit leaves all of them out. The citation narrowing I propose protects the trio but also makes the omission of the 3D story visible. I also accept that the 2016 prize leaves a legitimate question of increment, and the answer depends on a judgment about physics that Lindroth and Johansson may weigh differently from me. Finally, B006 is the configuration closest to my own field of band-structure theory, and I discount my preference for that reason.

responses.point: Kroll holds that optical lattice clocks are a distinct invention (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms), that their attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, and that the pending redefinition of the second should not delay the prize.
responses.response: I asked in round 1 whether the redefinition should matter, and your answer, that the Nobel criterion is the discovery and its demonstrated impact, is convincing. I withdraw that as an objection. I also accept your argument that magic-wavelength trapping addresses a different problem from the comb and from single-ion control, and I cannot refute it from outside precision metrology. Where we still differ is on how that distinctness weighs against B006, and here I am not making a claim about excellence: B047 is close to the top of the shortlist for me, which is why I have moved it to my first alternative. My reasons for preferring B006 are the breadth of its effect on how materials are calculated and measured, and the fact that its distinctness from 2016 is something I can argue directly. I cannot make an independent judgment about the clock's distinctness from 2005 and 2012, and I would not want my deference to you, or to Lindroth, to be the deciding factor.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B006 only as a first alternative because attribution is unresolved, and worries about the committee's appetite for a second topological prize after 2016.
responses.response: The attribution concern is mostly settled by the convergence you can see in the chair's summary: six members now name Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and the two earlier alternatives, Hasan for Mele or Hasan for Molenkamp, have been dropped by their original proponents or are held only as acceptable fallbacks. What remains is the cost of the omissions, which I acknowledge, but no three-name cut of this field would avoid it. The weakness of the 2016 argument is that it measures proximity by label. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topology in 1D chains and in quantum Hall states with broken time-reversal symmetry, while the Z2 state exists in a time-reversal-invariant system with spin-orbit coupling, a different symmetry class with different edge physics and different material candidates. If you still see a reduced appetite after that, I would like to hear whether it is about the physics or about the optics of a second topological prize in ten years, because I think only the first is a reason for me to change my view.

responses.point: Johansson says the increment over 2016 has to be argued, and says he could accept the Hasan version if colleagues find Mele's omission less costly.
responses.response: I have tried to give the one-sentence argument you asked for above, and I hope that resolves the increment question. On Hasan versus Mele, I still disagree with substituting him. Kane and Mele wrote the foundational Z2 and quantum spin Hall papers together, so removing Mele would split the theory half of the discovery and leave a citation that has to explain why only one theorist is named. The 3D photoemission observation matters, but it also depends on the Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents theory that is also left out, so replacing Mele with Hasan would not make the credit complete, only differently incomplete. The trio you and I both proposed in round 1 remains the more defensible cut, and I would accept your own citation wording about prediction and first observation without any change of substance.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp after round 1 and says he could accept the Hasan version if colleagues find Mele's omission less costly.
responses.response: I am glad we now name the same trio. I take your Hasan alternative seriously, because it is the strongest argument for extending the credit to the 3D materials discovery, and I do not think the omission of ARPES is trivial. But as I said to Johansson, the choice between Mele and Hasan is a choice between completeness on the theory side and an extension to materials. I would give more weight to the former because the prize is for a discovery that began as a theoretical one. If other members shift toward Hasan, I would ask that the citation then name both the quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D topological insulator explicitly, so it is clear that the 2D result is not being displaced.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, and in particular Lindroth and Johansson, accepts the symmetry-class argument as a sufficient increment over the 2016 prize.

Whether the HgTe proposers and Hasan can be omitted without a citation that appears to misstate where the theory-to-experiment path began. I have not independently checked the priority details of the early literature and rely on memory.
Whether B047's distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes is as strong as Kroll and Lindroth argue; I cannot judge this and so I did not use it as a reason against B047.

Whether my move from B017 to B006 and my present preference for B006 over B047 are partly the result of colleagues' arguments rather than independent assessment; I have tried to restate the reasons in my own terms.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional link to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye or any other credited person is apparent from my profile. My research on electronic structure, DFT and magnetism is close to the materials side of B006 and B017 and to B026, so I flag possible bias toward band-structure topics and have discounted it. As a member who chaired the 2025 cycle I have no further disclosure; this does not change from round 1.
